cues.text: In 1420, at the Royal Monastery of Santa Maria de Guadalupe in Extremadura, Spain, a priest found himself tempted to doubt transubstantiation during the celebration of Mass.
Later tradition names him Fray Pedro de Cabanuelas.
Transubstantiation is the Church's teaching that the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ at the words of consecration.
As the priest wrestled inwardly with this doubt, a dense cloud is said to have descended and settled above the altar itself.
Praying earnestly that his uncertainty be resolved, he watched the cloud give way to a vision of the consecrated Host suspended in the air above the chalice.

From the suspended Host, drops of Blood began to fall into the chalice below, until it overflowed and stained both the corporal and the pall — the small linen cloths used to cover and protect the sacred vessels during Mass.
Both cloths, bearing what tradition holds to be the marks of that overflow, have been preserved and venerated at the monastery ever since.
A Devotion That Reached a King
News of the event spread well beyond the walls of the monastery.
Among those whose faith it is said to have strengthened was the King of Castile himself—a detail that speaks to how quickly and widely such an event could travel through fifteenth-century Spain.
The relics were exhibited publicly for veneration during the Eucharistic Congress held at Toledo in 1926, drawing renewed attention to a story already five centuries old.
The stained corporal and pall remain objects of deep devotion among the Spanish faithful to this day, kept at one of Spain's most significant Marian and Eucharistic shrines.
Whatever one makes of the account’s precise historical texture, it belongs to a broader pattern common across this period and region.
A private, unspoken doubt was met not with condemnation but with a sign the doubting believer alone was given to see.
